tijdsregistratie_2027.title: Mandatory time registration in Belgium from 2027? What SMEs and employers need to know
tijdsregistratie_2027.lead: The federal government wants employers to record the working time their employees actually perform from 1 January 2027. The law is not there yet, but preparations are in full swing. This page explains what already applies today, what has been announced and how your SME can respond to this obligation in time.
tijdsregistratie_2027.updated: Last checked on 4 November 2026 · This page will be updated once the final law is published.

changes.title: The new legislation: what is coming?
paras: In the budget agreement of late November 2025, the federal government announced that all employers must record the working time their employees actually perform. The measure follows the European Working Time Directive and rulings of the Court of Justice, which require member states to impose an objective, reliable and accessible registration system.
changes.winprox: From day one you avoid disputes and limit the risk of administrative fines. WinProx is designed to help SMEs meet the announced requirements: automated and without the usual administrative hassle.
after: A preliminary draft bill was submitted to the National Labour Council on 30 September 2026, which issued a divided opinion. Entry into force is planned for 1 January 2027, with a practical implementation period until 1 April 2027 at the latest. Until the final vote in the Chamber the content may still change, but the message is to anticipate.

system.title: Why traditional systems fall short
paras: A simple Excel file or a traditional paper list is often no longer enough in a modern workplace. The government asks for objective, reliable data that cannot be changed unilaterally and that complies with strict privacy rules (GDPR).
system.winprox: The WinProx digital time clock records every clock action with a timestamp. On the clock screen the QR code keeps changing, which makes clocking hard to fake. The system is set up to be GDPR-compliant and gives you real-time insight into who is present.

sectors.intro: The obligation applies across sectors to employers in both the private and public sector, regardless of company size.

already.title: Which registration duties already apply today?
already.intro: There is no general registration duty for all hours yet, but there is a series of specific obligations:
items: Flexible working hours: anyone using them must already record actual performance.
Part-time work: all deviations from the fixed or variable schedule belong in a deviation register (to be kept for five years).
Sector-specific obligations: including Checkin@work on construction sites and attendance registration in cleaning.
already.note: If you already use a smart digital system, you are well prepared for the future general obligation.

prepare.intro: You do not have to wait for the final law to take useful steps:

Check whether your current approach (schedules, deviations, timesheets) is objective and reliable.
Make sure employees can easily report deviations or hours worked.
Seamless administration: WinProx exports the data so your social secretariat (such as SD Worx, Liantis or Acerta) can import it.
Inform employees in good time about the purpose and operation of the registration.

items.q: Is time registration already mandatory in Belgium today?
items.a: There is no general obligation, but there are specific duties — including gliding schedules, deviations from part-time schedules and sectoral attendance registration. The general duty is announced for 1 January 2027 but not yet enacted.

items.q: From when does the general obligation apply?
items.a: The draft provides for entry into force on 1 January 2027, with a practical deadline for employers to have their system operational by 1 April 2027 at the latest. The dates only become final once the law is passed.
No. The draft is technology-neutral: every employer chooses a system, as long as it records actual working time objectively and reliably.

items.q: Is recording only deviations from the schedule enough?
items.a: According to the draft, yes — provided the system can establish actual working time objectively and reliably. Employee organisations still contest this point in their opinion.

items.q: Does the obligation also apply to the public sector?
items.a: Yes, that is the intention. However, the public-sector text was not part of the draft submitted to the National Labour Council; a separate process will follow.

The draft excludes, among others, teleworkers, managerial and trust staff, sales representatives and mobile staff, but that list is not final yet. Do not assume a worker falls outside the duty on your own.

items.q: How long must the data be retained?
items.a: The government announced five years. The final retention period only follows in the enacted law.

items.q: What are the sanctions if I do nothing?
items.a: Sanctions and concrete enforcement have not been published yet — they follow with the final legislation.
